There is no evidence to suggest that enteropathogenic strains of E. coli respond differently to water treatment and disinfection compared to other E. coli strains. Therefore, conventional testing for E. coli or thermotolerant coliform bacteria serves as an appropriate indicator for the presence of enteropathogenic serotypes in drinking water, even though standard tests may not detect enterohemorrhagic E. coli (EHEC) strains. Helicobacter pylori (H. pylori), originally classified as Campylobacter pylori, is a Gram-negative, microaerophilic, spiral-shaped, motile bacterium. Among the 14 identified species of Helicobacter, only H. pylori is recognized as a human pathogen. It resides in the stomach and is often asymptomatic, but it is associated with chronic gastritis, peptic and duodenal ulcer disease, and gastric cancer. The role of H. pylori in causing these conditions remains unclear. Most infections begin in childhood and, if untreated, persist chronically. Infections are more prevalent in developing countries and are linked to overcrowded living conditions, with intrafamilial clustering being common. Humans are the primary host, though domestic cats may also serve as hosts. H. pylori has been detected in water and can survive for weeks in biofilms and surface waters, though it is unlikely to grow in the environment. Person-to-person transmission, particularly oral-oral, is the most likely route of infection, and fecal-oral transmission is also possible. Contaminated drinking water has been suggested as a potential source of infection, but further investigation is needed to confirm waterborne transmission. Klebsiella species are Gram-negative, non-motile bacilli that belong to the family Enterobacteriaceae. The genus includes species such as Klebsiella pneumoniae, Klebsiella oxytoca, Klebsiella planticola, and Klebsiella terrigena. These bacteria are characterized by a large polysaccharide capsule, which distinguishes them from other members of the family. Klebsiella pneumoniae and Klebsiella oxytoca are the most commonly isolated species from feces and clinical specimens and are known pathogens. These bacteria can cause serious infections, including destructive pneumonia, particularly in individuals with weakened immune systems, such as the elderly, very young, or those undergoing immunosuppressive therapy. Klebsiella species are natural inhabitants of water environments and can multiply in nutrient-rich waters. In drinking water systems, they are often biofilm organisms and are unlikely to pose a health risk to the general population. Legionella species, members of the family Legionellaceae, are Gram-negative, rod-shaped bacteria that require L-cysteine for growth. They are heterotrophic and thrive in water environments at temperatures above 25°C. Legionella pneumophila is the primary waterborne pathogen responsible for legionellosis, which includes Legionnaires’ disease (a severe pneumonia) and Pontiac fever (a milder, self-limiting illness). Risk factors for Legionnaires’ disease include smoking, alcohol abuse, chronic diseases, and immunosuppression. Legionella species are natural inhabitants of freshwater environments but thrive in human-made systems such as cooling towers, hot water systems, and spas. Infection typically occurs through inhalation of aerosols containing the bacteria. Leptospira interrogans causes leptospirosis, a zoonotic disease with a wide range of symptoms, from mild fever and headache to severe complications like jaundice, renal failure, and pulmonary hemorrhage. The disease is associated with contact with water contaminated by the urine of infected animals, such as rats and cattle. Leptospires can survive in water under favorable conditions and enter the body through cuts, abrasions, or mucous membranes. Non-tuberculous Mycobacterium species, such as Mycobacterium avium and Mycobacterium intracellulare, are natural inhabitants of water environments and can multiply in biofilms. These bacteria can cause a range of diseases, including pulmonary infections and disseminated infections in immunocompromised individuals. They are relatively resistant to disinfection, and their growth in biofilms reduces the effectiveness of disinfectants. Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a Gram-negative, aerobic bacterium that produces pigments such as pyocyanin and pyoverdin. It is commonly found in water environments and can cause infections, particularly in immunocompromised individuals.
